stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' claim?
stimulus: Public health researchers tested a program that sent text-message reminders about flu vaccination to adults in one county. Before the program began, each participant completed a survey stating whether they intended to be vaccinated that season. Vaccination rates among participants rose after the reminders were sent. The researchers claim that the reminders worked mainly by prompting people who already intended to be vaccinated to follow through, not by persuading people who had not planned to be vaccinated.
choices: Participants who received the reminders were vaccinated at a higher rate than similar adults in the county who received no reminders.
Among participants who had planned to be vaccinated, rates rose sharply, while among those who had not, rates barely changed.
Participants who had not planned to be vaccinated became much more likely to be vaccinated after receiving the reminders.
Most participants reported in a follow-up survey that the reminder messages had been clear and easy to understand.
explanation: The claim is about *who* the reminders affected: people who already intended to get vaccinated, not people who didn't. For support, the rise has to show up among intenders and be missing among non-intenders. Choice B shows exactly that split, so if it's true you would believe the claim more.

A.why: You picked a finding that shows the reminders worked at all. The claim goes further and says how they worked, and this choice doesn't separate intenders from non-intenders, so it supports a broader idea than the one claimed.

C.why: You matched the topic but missed the direction. If non-intenders were persuaded, the reminders did change minds, which is the very thing the researchers say did not happen.

D.why: You chose an on-topic fact about the messages. Whether they were clear says nothing about which group of participants they moved.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires parsing a distinction between prompting intended behavior vs. persuading new behavior, then matching to supporting data

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hollós's claim?
stimulus: Sediment cores show that a river near a Bronze Age settlement in the Carpathian Basin shifted its course around 1400 BCE, the same period in which the settlement was abandoned. Archaeologist Réka Hollós argues that the shift drove residents away not by flooding their homes but by raising the local water table, which spoiled the grain they stored in pits dug beneath their house floors.
choices: The house floors are covered by a thick layer of silt of the kind a river leaves behind after it floods.
Several other settlements along the same river were also abandoned at some point around 1400 BCE.
Residents of the settlement grew both barley and wheat, which were the main crops throughout the region.
The storage pits contain grain showing signs of water damage, while the floors above show no flood deposits.
explanation: Hollós's claim is a chain: the river shifted, the water table rose, the stored grain spoiled, and the residents left. She also rules out flooding. Choice D supports the middle link (water-damaged grain in the pits) and the exclusion (no flood deposits on the floors), so it backs her specific explanation.

A.why: You missed the phrase 'not by flooding their homes.' Flood silt on the floors would support the very explanation Hollós rejects.

B.why: You chose support for a broader idea, that the river shift somehow caused abandonment. It says nothing about spoiled grain in storage pits, which is the mechanism Hollós actually proposes.

C.why: You picked an accurate-sounding fact about the settlement's grain. Which crops the residents grew doesn't show whether rising groundwater spoiled them.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires understanding the mechanism (water table rise vs. flooding) and recognizing which evidence directly supports the claim

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vos's conclusion?
stimulus: A museum holds twelve impressions of a seventeenth-century woodcut showing a harbor scene, all attributed to a single Dutch workshop. Because the impressions are undated, scholars have long assumed they were pulled in one printing session. Art historian Mireille Vos disagrees, concluding that the impressions were printed from the same block over a span of several decades rather than all at once.
choices: The impressions are on sheets whose watermarks come from paper mills that operated in different decades.
The impressions share identical outlines and details, showing that they were all printed from one block.
The woodcut's harbor scene closely resembles harbor scenes painted by artists working in the same city.
Records from the workshop show that it held a single large printing session for the woodcut in 1652.
explanation: The key term in Vos's conclusion is 'over a span of several decades.' If the sheets came from mills that operated in different decades, the printing couldn't all have happened in one session, so Choice A directly supports her timing claim.

B.why: You supported only the uncontroversial half of the conclusion. Everyone already agrees the impressions came from one block. The dispute is about when they were printed, and identical details fit a single session just as well.

C.why: You chose an interesting fact about the image. Its resemblance to local paintings doesn't tell you when any impression was printed.

D.why: You matched the topic but reversed the claim. A record of a single printing session supports the older assumption that Vos rejects.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: straightforward identification of evidence for multiple printing sessions once you recognize watermark dating significance

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ashdown's claim?
stimulus: During the 1700s, weavers in one district of northern England largely abandoned wool in favor of linen. Linen required different spinning skills, but it could be woven on the same looms. Historian Thomas Ashdown claims that the change was driven by a shortage of local wool caused by disease among the district's sheep, not by a shift in what buyers wanted.
choices: Weavers in the district were able to weave linen on the same looms they had previously used for wool.
Buyers throughout England increasingly preferred linen garments to woolen ones during the 1700s.
The district's sheep numbers fell by half just before the change, while local demand for wool held steady.
Disease reduced sheep populations in many parts of Europe during the century before the change.
explanation: Ashdown's claim has two parts: a local wool shortage caused the switch, and buyer demand did not. Choice C supports both. The district's flocks shrank right before the change, and demand for wool stayed the same, which rules out a shift in taste.

A.why: You repeated a detail from the passage. Being able to reuse the looms made the switch easier, but it doesn't show that a wool shortage caused it.

B.why: You supported the rival explanation. A change in buyer preference is exactly what Ashdown says was not the cause.

D.why: You chose a broader, earlier fact. Disease elsewhere in Europe a century before doesn't show that this district's sheep declined when its weavers switched.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires distinguishing supply shortage from demand shift and identifying evidence supporting the causal claim

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?
stimulus: Astronomers have recorded repeated episodes in which a distant star dims for several weeks. Dust lying between a star and observers blocks blue light more strongly than infrared light, whereas a drop in a star's own energy output dims all wavelengths by roughly the same amount. A team studying the star concluded that its dimming is caused by an orbiting dust cloud passing in front of it rather than by changes in the star itself.
choices: During the most recent episode, the star's total brightness dropped by roughly 20 percent.
During each episode, the star dimmed about three times as much in blue light as in infrared.
During each episode, the star dimmed by about the same amount in blue light as in infrared.
Several other stars in the same region of the sky have also been observed dimming for weeks.
explanation: The passage tells you how to test the claim: dust dims blue light more than infrared, and changes in the star itself dim both equally. Uneven dimming, stronger in blue, points to dust, so Choice B supports the team's conclusion.

A.why: You chose a fact about how much the star dimmed. The size of the drop doesn't separate dust from a change in the star, because only the difference between wavelengths does that.

C.why: You reversed the test. According to the passage, equal dimming at both wavelengths points to a change in the star itself, which is the explanation the team rejects.

D.why: You were drawn by topic overlap. Other stars dimming says nothing about what causes this star to dim.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires understanding the physical distinction between dust blocking (wavelength-selective) and energy loss (uniform), then matching to data

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the planners' claim?
stimulus: Curb extensions widen the sidewalk at a street corner, shortening the distance pedestrians must walk to cross. After a city added curb extensions at forty intersections, its planners reviewed five years of injury reports. The planners claim that curb extensions reduce pedestrian injuries at intersections with heavy traffic, even if they do little at quiet intersections.
choices: At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell 40 percent after extensions were added but held steady at similar ones without them.
Across all of the city's intersections, pedestrian injuries fell by about 8 percent during the five years reviewed.
At quiet intersections, pedestrian injury counts were about the same before and after curb extensions were added.
At high-traffic intersections, injuries fell by similar amounts whether or not curb extensions had been added.
explanation: The scope words are 'at intersections with heavy traffic.' To support the claim, a finding has to show a drop at busy intersections that can be credited to the extensions. Choice A shows a large drop where extensions were added and none at comparable intersections without them.

B.why: You ignored the scope words. A small citywide drop includes intersections without extensions and says nothing about busy intersections specifically.

C.why: You supported only the 'even if' concession. Showing that extensions did little at quiet corners doesn't show that they helped at busy ones, which is the actual claim.

D.why: You overlooked the comparison. If injuries fell just as much without extensions, something other than the extensions caused the drop, which undercuts the claim.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires parsing a conditional claim about differential effects at different intersection types and finding the specific supporting pattern

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tuilagi's claim?
stimulus: Younger speakers of a language spoken on several islands in the western Pacific have largely stopped using a set of honorific verb forms that their grandparents use routinely. Linguist Ana Tuilagi claims that this loss stems from the decline of the ceremonial gatherings where those forms were mainly heard, rather than from young people's growing use of English.
choices: Young speakers throughout the islands now speak English fluently and use it every day at school.
The honorific verb forms are used mainly when a speaker is addressing a chief or an elder.
The young speakers who use English most at school are the least likely to use the honorific forms.
Where gatherings are still held often, young people use the forms as much as elders, despite equal English use.
explanation: Tuilagi separates two possible causes and credits the decline of gatherings. Choice D works like a natural experiment. Where gatherings survive, young people keep the forms even though their English use is the same, which points to gatherings and not English.

A.why: You chose a true-sounding background fact. Widespread English use doesn't tell you whether English or the decline of gatherings caused the loss, and if anything it leans toward the rival explanation.

B.why: You picked an accurate detail about the forms themselves. Knowing who they are used for doesn't show why young people stopped using them.

C.why: You supported the explanation Tuilagi rejects. A link between heavy English use and losing the forms points to English, not to the decline of gatherings.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: requires isolating contextual factors from language contact and recognizing what evidence would eliminate the English explanation

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus: Song sparrows living in cities tend to sing at higher pitches than rural song sparrows do, but cities differ from the countryside in many ways besides noise. To isolate one factor, researchers raised two groups of sparrow chicks in identical aviaries; in one, recorded traffic noise played throughout the day, and the other was kept quiet. The researchers hypothesize that low-frequency traffic noise itself causes young sparrows to develop higher-pitched songs.
choices: Song sparrows in large cities sing at higher pitches than song sparrows in nearby rural areas.
Birds raised in the two aviaries began producing recognizable songs at about the same age.
As adults, birds from the noisy aviary sang with noticeably higher pitches than birds from the quiet one.
As adults, birds from the two aviaries sang at nearly identical pitches regardless of the noise.
explanation: The aviaries differ in only one way: traffic noise. If the hypothesis is right, the birds from the noisy aviary should sing higher. Decide that direction first, and Choice C is the finding that matches it.

A.why: You fell for the on-topic trap. The passage already says city birds sing higher, and it points out that cities differ in many ways. This fact can't show that noise in particular is the cause, which is why the experiment was needed.

B.why: You chose a finding about when the birds started singing. The hypothesis is about pitch, so the age at which songs appeared doesn't bear on it.

D.why: You got the direction backward. Identical pitches across the two aviaries would suggest noise has no effect, which weakens the hypothesis.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: straightforward experimental interpretation once you recognize what results would support the noise hypothesis

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's claim?
stimulus: Wheat fields bordered by hedgerows often have less aphid damage than fields bordered by open fencing. Hedgerows slow the wind that carries aphids into crops, and they also shelter ground beetles that crawl out at night and eat aphids on nearby wheat. Ecologist Nadia Ferreira claims that hedgerows reduce aphid damage mainly because they shelter beetles, not because they block wind.
choices: Hedgerows that were fenced off at ground level to keep beetles from leaving had almost no effect on aphid damage in neighboring wheat.
Wheat fields bordered by hedgerows had lower aphid damage on average than wheat fields of the same size bordered by open fencing.
Wheat fields sheltered from wind by tall stone walls had as little aphid damage as wheat fields bordered by hedgerows.
Hedgerows bordering wheat fields shelter many kinds of insects, including bees that pollinate wildflowers growing nearby.
explanation: Ferreira's claim is about which mechanism matters: beetles rather than blocked wind. A barrier that keeps beetles in removes only the beetle effect and leaves the wind effect in place. If aphid damage then goes back up, the beetles must have been doing most of the work. That is the exact claim.

B.why: This is on topic and true, but the passage already says hedgerows reduce damage. Ferreira's claim is about why they do. This finding fits the beetle explanation and the wind explanation equally well, so it can't tell you which one matters more.

C.why: Stone walls block wind but don't shelter beetles. If walls protect wheat as well as hedgerows do, then blocking wind is enough on its own. That points to wind, which is the reverse of Ferreira's claim.

D.why: This is an accurate fact about hedgerows, but bees and wildflowers have nothing to do with aphids or beetles. It leaves the claim untouched.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's claim?
stimulus: Excavations at a 3,000-year-old village have turned up two kinds of pottery: plain, thick-walled cooking pots and thin, painted serving jars. Similar painted jars appear at many sites across the region, so most researchers think the jars were acquired through trade. Archaeologist Daniel Okafor accepts that view of the jars but concludes that the village's cooking pots, at least, were made by the villagers themselves.
choices: The clay in the painted serving jars has the same mineral composition as a clay bed located just outside the village.
Black soot coats the outer surfaces of most of the village's cooking pots, which shows that they were used over open fires.
The clay in the cooking pots matches a clay bed beside the village and differs from clay used at other sites in the region.
Cooking pots matching the village's in shape and thickness were found in older layers at a coastal site 200 kilometers away.
explanation: Okafor's claim is narrow: the cooking pots, specifically, were made locally. If their clay matches a bed right beside the village and doesn't match clay from elsewhere, the pots were most likely made at the village. That directly supports the claim.

A.why: This finding is about the wrong group of objects. Okafor's claim concerns the cooking pots, not the painted jars, so evidence about the jars leaves the claim untouched.

B.why: This tells you how the pots were used, not where they were made. A pot brought in by trade could be just as sooty. It's on topic but doesn't address the claim.

D.why: If identical pots show up earlier at a distant site, the design probably started there and may have reached the village through trade. That cuts against Okafor's claim instead of supporting it.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the economists' claim?
stimulus: When a city raised its minimum wage from $12 to $15 an hour, economists compared fast-food restaurants inside the city limits with similar restaurants just outside them, where the wage floor stayed at $12. Turnover fell at the city restaurants. The economists claim that the drop happened mainly among workers whose pay the new law actually raised.
choices: Restaurants inside the city raised their menu prices more in the following year than restaurants just outside the city did.
In city restaurants, turnover fell among workers who had been paid under $15 but stayed flat among those already paid more.
Turnover fell by about the same amount at restaurants just outside the city as it did at restaurants inside the city.
Raising a minimum wage lowers worker turnover in every industry and region where such an increase has been put in place.
explanation: Pin down the scope of the claim first. It isn't just that turnover fell. It says turnover fell mainly among workers whose pay went up. If turnover dropped only for workers who had been earning under $15, and not for those the law didn't affect, the drop is concentrated exactly where the claim says it should be.

A.why: Menu prices are another plausible effect of the wage increase, but they say nothing about which workers stopped leaving. The choice is on topic but doesn't address the claim.

C.why: Wages outside the city didn't change. If turnover fell just as much there, the drop wasn't caused by the raise at all. That undermines the economists' explanation.

D.why: This is a much broader claim than the economists made. Even if it were true, it wouldn't show that the drop in this city was concentrated among workers whose pay rose.

subtype_name: Which finding, if true, supports the claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's conclusion?
stimulus: When a regional grocery chain raised its starting wage from $14 to $17 an hour at half of its stores, economist Lena Okafor compared those stores with the chain's otherwise similar stores that kept the old wage. Higher pay, she reasoned, makes a job costlier to lose, so fewer workers quit, and a store that loses fewer workers has fewer replacements to train. Okafor concluded that the raise lowered training costs at the higher-wage stores.
choices: Workers at the higher-wage stores reported greater job satisfaction after the raise than before it, especially among cashiers.
Across the national retail industry, firms paying above the regional average wage report lower turnover than other firms.
Over the next year, the higher-wage stores lost fewer workers and spent less on training per store than the other stores did.
Both groups of stores lost similar numbers of workers that year, but the higher-wage stores drew more applicants per opening.
explanation: Okafor's claim is about a gap: training costs at the higher-wage stores compared with the stores that kept the old wage. Her reasoning runs from higher pay to fewer quits to less training. Choice C confirms both the middle link (fewer departures) and the final result (lower training spending), and it compares the two groups of stores directly. If C were true, you would believe the claim more.

A.why: This choice is about the right stores and the right raise, but job satisfaction says nothing about quits or training costs. You picked a true-sounding fact on the topic that leaves the claim itself untouched.

B.why: This is a broad finding about the whole retail industry, and it is only about turnover. It can't show what happened to training costs at this chain's two groups of stores. You accepted support for a wider, neighbouring idea.

D.why: If departures were about the same in both groups, the link Okafor relies on (higher pay leads to fewer quits) breaks. This choice cuts against her reasoning. More applicants doesn't mean fewer people to train.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus: Vaccines tend to work less well in older animals, partly because their dendritic cells, which show vaccine material to other immune cells, mature slowly. An experimental adjuvant, a compound added to vaccines, speeds dendritic-cell maturation. A research team vaccinated young and old mice, with and without the adjuvant. The researchers hypothesize that the adjuvant will narrow the gap in antibody levels between old and young mice.
choices: Old mice given the adjuvant produced more antibodies than old mice vaccinated without it, and they did so within a week.
Without the adjuvant, old mice made about a third as many antibodies as young mice; with it, about four-fifths as many.
Dendritic cells from old mice matured more slowly than those of young mice, whether or not the adjuvant was given.
Old mice given the adjuvant stayed protected against infection longer than young mice vaccinated without it did.
explanation: The hypothesis is about a gap, the difference between old and young mice, and it predicts that the gap shrinks when the adjuvant is added. Choice B gives the old-to-young ratio under both conditions: it rises from about one-third to about four-fifths. That is the gap narrowing, which is exactly what the researchers predicted.

A.why: This choice only compares old mice with other old mice. The adjuvant could boost young mice just as much, which would leave the gap unchanged. You answered about one group instead of the difference between the two groups.

C.why: The passage says the adjuvant speeds dendritic-cell maturation. A finding that old cells stayed slow with the adjuvant goes against the mechanism the hypothesis depends on, so it doesn't support it.

D.why: This choice compares mismatched groups (treated old mice against untreated young mice) and measures how long protection lasts, not antibody levels. It says nothing about the old-versus-young gap under the same treatment, so you read more into it than it shows.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the seismologist's claim?
stimulus: Part of a mountain city sits on an ancient lakebed filled with soft clay, while nearby districts rest on bedrock hills. Seismic waves slow down when they pass from rock into soft clay, and slower waves grow taller, so the ground they cross moves more. Pointing to this process, a seismologist claims that during any given earthquake, ground on the basin floor shakes much harder than ground on the surrounding hills.
choices: The clay filling the basin is thickest near its center, where it reaches depths of more than forty meters below the surface.
In a nineteenth-century earthquake, many more buildings collapsed in the basin districts than in the hillside districts.
During one recent earthquake centered beneath the hills, hillside instruments recorded stronger shaking than basin instruments.
In each of three recent earthquakes, basin-floor instruments recorded about three times the peak ground motion of hillside ones.
explanation: The claim compares two places during the same earthquake: the basin floor should shake much harder than the hills. Choice D measures that gap directly, in three separate quakes, with instruments in both places, and finds basin motion about three times hillside motion. If D were true, you would believe the claim more.

A.why: This is an accurate-sounding detail about the basin, but clay depth on its own says nothing about how hard the basin shakes compared with the hills. It is on topic but doesn't touch the claim.

B.why: Building collapse depends on construction quality and age, not only on ground motion. Treating damage as a measurement of shaking reads more into this finding than it can show.

C.why: This finding has the comparison going the wrong way: the hills shook harder than the basin. That cuts against the seismologist's claim rather than supporting it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support the team's conclusion?
stimulus: At Tell Varek, a Bronze Age village in present-day Turkey, archaeologists recovered dozens of basalt grinding stones from the floors of houses. Some scholars have argued that small villages in the region obtained most of their flour already milled, trading for it with larger towns nearby. After studying the Tell Varek houses, however, archaeologist Leyla Durmaz's team concluded that residents there ground their own grain at home rather than relying on imported flour.
choices: Charred husks and chaff, the waste left when grain is cleaned for grinding, were concentrated on the house floors.
The grinding stones recovered from the houses showed heavy surface wear consistent with long, repeated use.
Storage pits inside the houses held whole wheat kernels but contained no traces of already milled flour.
Grinding stones found in the larger nearby towns were cut from the same type of basalt as those at Tell Varek.
explanation: The claim is narrow: Tell Varek's residents ground grain at home instead of importing flour. Ask of each choice, 'If this were true, would I believe that more?' Choice D is about grinding stones somewhere else. Shared basalt tells you nothing about where Tell Varek's flour was made, and it could even hint at trade between the village and the towns. It's on topic, but it doesn't touch the claim, so it's the one that fails to support it.

A.why: You may have read this as a detail about cleaning grain rather than milling it. But chaff only builds up where whole grain is processed. Finding it on the house floors shows that grain came into the houses unmilled, which supports the claim.

B.why: You may have thought this only shows the stones existed, which the passage already says. Heavy wear shows they were used often and over a long time. That's what you'd expect if residents milled their own grain, so it supports the conclusion.

C.why: You may have dismissed this as a fact about storage rather than grinding. But households that stored whole kernels and no flour had to mill the grain themselves, so this backs the claim directly.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support Okafor's claim?
stimulus: To test whether sleeping at simulated high altitude improves endurance, sports scientist Ana Okafor recruited 24 competitive cyclists with similar training histories. For six weeks, half slept in tents filled with reduced-oxygen air, and half slept in identical tents with normal air. Both groups followed the same training schedule. The reduced-oxygen group's endurance improved more, and Okafor claims that this gain occurred because the reduced oxygen raised the riders' red blood cell concentrations.
choices: The reduced-oxygen group's red blood cell concentrations rose, while the normal-air group's stayed the same.
Within the reduced-oxygen group, the riders with the largest red blood cell increases improved the most.
The reduced-oxygen group's endurance gains were larger than those reported in earlier studies of altitude camps.
Reduced-oxygen riders whose red blood cell levels did not rise showed no improvement in endurance.
explanation: Okafor isn't just saying the tents worked. Her claim is about the mechanism: reduced oxygen raised red blood cells, and that rise caused the endurance gain. To support it, a finding has to involve the middle link, red blood cells. Choice C only says the gains were big compared with other studies. It never mentions red blood cells, so it leaves the cause untouched.

A.why: You may have thought this only covers blood and says nothing about endurance. But it establishes the first link: reduced oxygen raised red blood cells, and only in the group whose endurance improved. That supports the mechanism.

B.why: You may have misread this as a comparison between groups that the passage already made. It actually shows that, within one group, a bigger red blood cell rise went with a bigger gain. That link between the two is exactly what the claim needs.

D.why: You may have read 'no improvement' as evidence against the study. Look again: if riders who slept in the same tents but had no red blood cell rise also had no gain, then the red blood cells are doing the work. That strongly supports the claim.

stem: Which finding, if true, would NOT support Lindqvist's hypothesis?
stimulus: Great tits living in cities sing at higher pitches than great tits living in forests. Cities differ from forests in many ways, including temperature, food supply, and noise, and traffic noise in particular is concentrated at low frequencies that can drown out low notes. Biologist Hans Lindqvist hypothesizes that urban great tits' higher songs are a response specifically to traffic noise rather than to other features of city life.
choices: Within a single city, great tits nesting beside busy roads sing higher than those nesting in quiet parks.
Great tits in cities on several continents sing higher than great tits in the forests near those cities.
Individual great tits sing higher on weekdays, when traffic is heavy, than on the quieter weekends.
Forest great tits exposed to recordings of traffic noise begin singing at higher pitches than before.
explanation: The key word is 'specifically.' Lindqvist has to show that traffic noise, and not warmth, food, or anything else about cities, drives the higher pitch. Choice B only repeats the city-versus-forest difference on a larger scale. City birds still differ from forest birds in every way the passage lists, so B supports a broader idea (cities change songs) but not the narrower claim that traffic noise is the cause.

A.why: You may have thought a comparison inside one city misses the city-versus-forest question. That's actually its strength. Both groups of birds live in the same city, so the main thing that differs is traffic, which isolates noise as the cause.

C.why: You may have thought this is about the days of the week rather than about noise. But the same birds in the same place sing higher only when traffic is heavy. Everything else stays the same, so the change points to traffic noise.

D.why: You may have dismissed this because the birds are in a forest, not a city. That's the point: the only city feature they got was traffic noise, and their pitch still rose. That's direct support for the hypothesis.
